title: Health checks turn a dead server into a non-event
description: A load balancer is only as good as its idea of 'healthy'. When a server fails its check it leaves the pool, and the users who would have hit it notice nothing.

nodes.label: Check what this instance controls
nodes.sublabel:
A check that verifies a shared
database fails on every instance
at once — removing the whole
fleet and turning a degraded
dependency into an outage.

steps.text: Clients address the load balancer, never an individual server. That indirection is what makes the next step invisible to them.
Server 2 stops passing its health check. The balancer stops sending it traffic — the dashed line is a path no longer taken, not a broken request.
Its share is absorbed by the survivors. Capacity drops by a third; availability does not change at all. This is the difference between a capacity event and an outage.
If sessions were pinned to Server 2, its users do not fail over gracefully — their session state died with the machine and they are logged out.
With a stateless tier and session state in a shared store, any server can serve any request, so a failure costs capacity rather than user sessions. That is the whole argument for statelessness.
